documentation for wis, the browser that sees everything and tells nothing.

wis is an open-source, fast, safe and lightweight browser for macOS. it renders
with the same WebKit engine your mac already runs, so there is no second browser
engine to bundle, update, or feed memory to. what you get instead is a tiny
download, low RAM use, Safari-class speed and battery, and a privacy stack built
in rather than bolted on.

these docs cover how to install wis, every feature it ships, and the honest
tradeoffs that come with building on the system WebView.

## start here

- [install wis](/docs/getting-started/installation/) for macOS, or build it
  yourself on Linux and Windows.
- [build from source](/docs/getting-started/building-from-source/) with the
  Makefile.

## features

privacy and blocking run by default: trackers blocked at the engine, DNS over
HTTPS, HTTPS-First, cosmetic filtering, and a built-in Tor toggle. on top of
that sit workspaces, split panes, tab folders, a Touch ID password vault, link
previews, custom themes, and more. browse the **features** section in the
sidebar, or jump to a few highlights:

- [workspaces](/docs/features/workspaces/): color-accented profiles, each with
  its own session, proxy, and privacy mode.
- [tabs and panes](/docs/features/tabs-and-panes/): folders, pins, tmux-style
  splits, and sessions that survive a restart.
- [privacy and blocking](/docs/features/privacy-and-blocking/): the native
  blocking stack that replaces extensions.
- [network and Tor](/docs/features/network-and-tor/): DoH, HTTPS-First, and the
  one-toggle Tor VPN.

## reference

- [keyboard shortcuts](/docs/reference/keyboard-shortcuts/): every default
  binding, all rebindable.
- [known limitations](/docs/reference/known-limitations/): what the WebKit
  engine cannot do, stated plainly.
- [architecture](/docs/reference/architecture/): how wis is built, for
  contributors.

light and dark themes pushed to web content, full custom themes you can build and share, layouts, and motion controls.

wis is yours to shape. layouts, themes, motion, and per-workspace backgrounds
all live in **settings → appearance** and **settings → layout**.

## light, dark, and system

the light/dark/system setting drives the whole chrome, and wis **pushes it to web
content too**: each page's native appearance is overridden so a site's
`prefers-color-scheme` matches your in-app theme instead of the OS. set wis to
dark and pages render dark, even if your mac is in light mode.

## layouts

choose between a collapsible **sidebar** and a horizontal **top-tabs** strip. the
sidebar can float and auto-expand on hover; toggle it with **Cmd+S**. the
top-tabs strip behaves as an accordion, keeping at most a set number of folders
expanded at once (configurable in **settings → layout**).

## custom themes

build a full chrome theme in **settings → appearance → themes**. a theme carries
both light and dark token sets, accent plus backgrounds, surfaces, text, and
borders. the accent expands into the full color scale automatically, so the
entire chrome re-themes live as you edit.

- create, duplicate, and delete themes, with per-mode color pickers and live
  preview.
- **share** a theme: export it to a `.wistheme` file and import one back. imports
  are validated and given a fresh id, so a shared theme never collides with one
  you already have.

## per-workspace backgrounds

each workspace can carry its own gradient, wallpaper, or GIF background.
see [workspaces → per-workspace backgrounds](/docs/features/workspaces/#per-workspace-backgrounds)
for the details.

## motion

a three-level motion setting in **settings → appearance** controls chrome
animation:

- **full**: every transition, including the springy ones.
- **reduced**: keeps timings but flattens the overshoot.
- **off**: zeroes chrome transition and animation durations.

your OS "reduce motion" preference caps full at reduced automatically, live.

per-workspace bookmarks with folders, a quick-access pinned row, and drag-to-organise.

bookmarks in wis are per-workspace and can be organised into optional folders.
they are stored separately from your browsing state and never leave the
workspace they belong to. bookmarks are disabled in private (ephemeral)
workspaces.

## saving a page

the **star** in the address bar bookmarks the current page. it saves into the
last folder you used, auto-pins the page to the quick-access row while that row
has space, and then opens a small folder picker so you can confirm or change
where it lives. clicking the star again removes the bookmark.

you can also bookmark with **Cmd+Shift+B**, which drives the same star flow.
(Cmd+B is deliberately left to pages for bold text.)

## the bookmarks popup

a bookmarks glyph in the sidebar footer (or the top-tabs rail) opens a
palette-style popup, openable any time with **Alt+Cmd+B**. it shows, in order:

1. the **pinned quick-access grid**, every pinned bookmark.
2. **folders**, each expanding to its bookmarks.
3. the **unfiled and unpinned** rest, below the folders.

## organising

everything in the popup is drag-and-drop:

- drag a favicon **onto a folder** to file it (it stays pinned if it was).
- drag it **onto the unfiled area** to take it out of a folder.
- drag it **onto the pinned grid** to pin it, or drop it on a pinned bubble to
  replace that slot when the row is full.
- drag favicons **onto each other inside a folder** to reorder them.
- drag a folder's **grip handle** to reorder folders.

right-click a bookmark for pin/unpin and a "move to" menu. **pinning is
independent of folder membership**: a bookmark can be pinned to the quick-access
grid and still live in a folder, appearing in both. folder create, rename, and
delete are inline (deleting a folder re-files its bookmarks as unfiled).

safety-first downloads with a popup, a full history page, and an optional "ask where to save".

wis handles downloads safety-first. files always land in `~/Downloads` by
default, with safe names, no overwrites, and the same Gatekeeper scanning any
browser download gets.

## how it handles a file

- the server-suggested filename is reduced to a **safe leaf** (final path
  component only, no control characters, no escaping the downloads folder) and
  collision-resolved Finder-style, so a download never overwrites an existing
  file.
- completed files are tagged with the macOS **quarantine** attribute, so
  Gatekeeper scans them like any browser download.
- downloads from a **private workspace or peek** still save (you asked for them)
  but are flagged private and never recorded in history.

## the downloads popup

a downloads glyph sits in both layouts (the sidebar footer and the top-tabs
rail), with a pulsing dot while anything is in flight. open it any time with
**Cmd+J**. it shows the latest items:

- in-flight rows with a live byte count.
- completed rows that **open the file** on click, or show "file may have been
  moved or deleted" when it is gone.
- an X to remove an entry from the list.
- a "view all downloads" footer that opens the full page.

## the downloads page

the full page (`about:downloads`) adds search over filename and URL, day
grouping, per-row **open** and **show in Finder**, and a select mode whose delete
removes only history entries, never the files themselves. completed downloads
persist across restarts.

## ask where to save

turn on **settings → downloads → "ask where to save"** to get a native save
panel for every download, prefilled with the safe name and starting in the last
folder you picked. cancelling the panel cancels the download.

float a playing video as an always-on-top mini player, and see and mute audio per tab.

## video popout

switch away from a tab that is playing a video and wis floats that video as an
always-on-top mini player in its own window, free to leave the main browser
window and visible on every macOS Space. it is the same video, not a copy: wis
moves the tab's own webview into the floating window and back, so even streams
that cannot be re-opened elsewhere keep playing.

the mini player has its own controls:

- click to **play or pause**; double-click the left or right third to **seek
  -/+10 seconds**.
- a hover-revealed **volume cluster** mutes, sets the level, and stays in lockstep
  with the site's own player both ways.
- **drag** anywhere to move it; drag a corner to resize, locked to the video's
  aspect ratio.
- an **X** top-right pauses and dismisses it (it pauses first, so audio never
  plays invisibly).

popout works two ways:

- **automatic**: when you leave a tab whose video is actually playing, it floats.
  controlled by **settings → layout** (on by default). muted autoplay ads do not
  trigger it.
- **manual**: a small pop-out button on the video under your cursor, or the
  **pop out video** action (Cmd+Shift+O, rebindable). manual popouts work for
  paused videos too and leave the tab's pane in place with a black placeholder
  you can click to fold the video back.

one video pops out at a time. the popped tab is exempt from sleeping. note that
only main-frame videos pop out; a video embedded in a cross-origin iframe does
not.

## tab audio and mute

any tab that is audibly playing shows a **speaker** beside its favicon, in both
the sidebar and the top-tabs strip, using the same signal Safari's tab icon
does, so iframe players and Web Audio count too.

click the speaker to **mute** the tab without activating it. a muted tab shows a
slashed speaker whether or not it is currently making sound, so you can always
unmute it. muting is engine-level, so a page cannot un-mute itself. widget panels
get the same mute as a header-bar toggle.

audibly-playing tabs never sleep while they are making sound, so wis never cuts
your audio out from under you; they sleep normally once silent or muted.

DNS over HTTPS, HTTPS-First, the one-toggle built-in Tor VPN, upstream proxies, media extensions, and staying logged in across restarts.

wis treats the network as a privacy boundary. every request a workspace makes is
judged per workspace: blocked, upgraded, or routed through your proxy or Tor,
before it leaves the machine.

## DNS over HTTPS

DNS lookups are resolved over HTTPS (DoH), so the names you visit are not sent in
the clear for anyone on the network to read.

## HTTPS-First

wis enforces HTTPS-First: a plain `http://` request is upgraded to `https://`
before it leaves, so you connect securely wherever a site supports it.

## Tor VPN

wis has a **built-in Tor client** (Arti), exposed as a simple on/off toggle in
the sidebar and the top-tabs rail. there is no extension and no separate browser
to run.

- the Tor icon lights only when connected, and shows a connecting state in
  between.
- toggling Tor re-routes the workspace by reloading its tabs.

Tor is a default build feature, so a standard build of wis already includes it.

## upstream proxy

each workspace can route through an upstream proxy, either a SOCKS5 endpoint or
the built-in Tor. the proxy is per workspace, so you can run one workspace over
Tor and another direct at the same time.

## media extensions (MSE and EME)

wis enables WebKit's Media Source Extensions and Encrypted Media Extensions on
pages, toggleable in **settings → privacy**.

- **MSE** restores adaptive streaming on many non-DRM video sites (it is off by
  default in an embedded WebKit).
- **EME** exposes the FairPlay key system to services that request it.

this does not unlock Widevine-gated services; see
[known limitations](/docs/reference/known-limitations/) for what the engine can
and cannot play, and the [open in default browser](/docs/features/productivity/#open-in-default-browser)
escape hatch for the rest.

## stay logged in across restarts

WebKit keeps session cookies (the kind with no expiry) only in memory and drops
them on quit, so logins like Canvas would not survive a restart. wis snapshots a
workspace's session cookies and restores them on its next launch, so you stay
signed in.

these snapshots are **encrypted at rest** with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a key in
the macOS Keychain, separate from the password vault and available automatically
at launch. because session cookies are live bearer tokens, a restored session
**auto-expires after 14 days**, forcing a periodic re-auth so a stolen snapshot
is only useful for a bounded window. ephemeral (private) workspaces never persist
anything.

turn it off in **settings → privacy → "stay logged in across restarts"** (on by
default); turning it off skips the snapshots and wipes any that were saved.

an encrypted password vault unlocked with Touch ID, with save-on-submit capture and origin-matched autofill.

wis includes a password vault: encrypted at rest, unlocked with Touch ID, and
fully on-device. pages can never reach it; only wis can read a credential, and
only to fill it into the page it belongs to.

## how it is secured

credentials are sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305 (AEAD) under a 32-byte master key.
that key is generated with the OS random generator, stored in the macOS login
Keychain as this-device-only, and released into memory only after a **Touch ID**
check. the in-memory copy is wiped as soon as it is no longer needed, and
plaintext is never logged or written to disk.

## saving a password

when you submit a login, wis offers to save it. the capture watches several
submit signals, form submit, Enter in a password field, a click on a login
button, the page tearing down, and the password field disappearing, and it
pierces shadow DOM, so it catches single-page-app and modal logins (Twitch,
Gmail, Canvas) that a naive form watcher would miss.

the save prompt follows the login you captured across the post-login navigation,
so it waits for you to act instead of vanishing when the page changes.

## autofill

the **key button** in the address bar surfaces the logins saved for the current
site. wis matches credentials to the page origin and fills them by evaluating
into the page; the page itself can never call the vault. hosts are normalised so
a login saved on `www.example.com` still fills on `example.com` and vice versa.

## managing saved logins

manage everything in **settings → passwords**: view saved accounts, and remove
ones you no longer need.

the native blocking stack that replaces extensions, tracker blocking, cosmetic filtering, an element picker, scriptlets, filter lists, and user scripts.

an embedded WebKit cannot load browser extensions, so wis ships a **native
blocking stack** instead. it runs by default, with no add-ons to install, and
covers most of what an ad blocker plus a userscript manager would.

## tracker and ad blocking

trackers are blocked at two levels: host-level blocking in the per-workspace
network proxy, and engine-level blocking compiled into a WebKit content-rule
list. wis ships with EasyPrivacy and EasyList, refreshed in the background and
cached so a warm launch never re-parses them.

blocking is skipped for workspaces set to **permissive** privacy mode.

## cosmetic filtering

network blocking stops requests, but it leaves behind empty ad slots,
placeholders, and overlay nags. cosmetic filtering hides those: wis applies the
filter lists' element-hiding rules to each page, including modern `:has(...)`
rules that catch containers like sponsored feed cards. it re-applies itself
across single-page-app navigations, so sites that swap content without a full
reload stay clean.

## element picker and zapper

when something slips through, hide it yourself. open the picker with
**Cmd+Shift+X** (or **view → hide element**), hover to highlight the element
under your cursor, and click to hide it. wis computes a stable selector, hides it
immediately, and remembers it for that site on every future visit.

manage hidden elements in **settings → privacy → filter lists** (the "hidden
elements" list).

## filter lists

**settings → privacy → filter lists** manages your subscriptions. wis defaults
to the uBO filters and quick-fixes lists (which carry the YouTube rules), and you
can add or remove any HTTPS filter-list URL. each is fetched, cached, and folded
into the blocking engine; adding one triggers a fetch and rebuild that re-applies
to live tabs.

**scriptlets** from Brave's prebuilt uBO resource library expand `+js(...)` rules
into small injected scripts. this is what makes **YouTube ad blocking** work:
the scriptlets strip ad entries from the player's responses before they play.

## user scripts

wis includes a Tampermonkey-style user-script runner. import a `.user.js` file
in **settings → privacy → user scripts**, and wis reads its `==UserScript==`
metadata (`@name`, `@match`, `@include`, `@exclude`, `@run-at`) to decide where
and when it runs.

:::note
user scripts run in the **page world with no GM_* APIs**. they are good for DOM
and CSS tweaks and self-contained logic; they do not get a privileged bridge.
each script is wrapped so an error in one cannot break the page.
:::

scripts are skipped in permissive workspaces, like the rest of the blocking
stack. toggle or remove them any time.

## fraudulent website warning

every page wis loads has WebKit's fraudulent-website warning enabled (Apple's
proxied Safe Browsing). it shows a full-page warning before a suspected phishing
or malware site, backed by a real threat database, complementing the structural
heuristics in [safe browsing](/docs/features/safe-browsing/). toggle it in
**settings → privacy** (it is on by default, since the check performs network
lookups).

an embedded WebKit cannot load browser extensions, so wis ships a native blocking stack instead. it runs by default, with no add-ons to install, and covers most of what an ad blocker plus a userscript manager would.

tracker and ad blocking

Section titled “tracker and ad blocking”

blocking is skipped for workspaces set to permissive privacy mode.

Section titled “cosmetic filtering”

network blocking stops requests, but it leaves behind empty ad slots, placeholders, and overlay nags. cosmetic filtering hides those: wis applies the filter lists’ element-hiding rules to each page, including modern :has(...) rules that catch containers like sponsored feed cards. it re-applies itself across single-page-app navigations, so sites that swap content without a full reload stay clean.

Section titled “element picker and zapper”

Section titled “filter lists”

itself the default browser, it falls back to Safari so the handoff cannot loop
back in.

it, along with cookies and other site data, from the unified clear-browsing-data
dialog (**Cmd+Shift+Backspace**).

peek at links in an isolated preview, a navigation safety interstitial for risky links, and per-site camera and microphone consent.

beyond the [fraudulent-website warning](/docs/features/privacy-and-blocking/#fraudulent-website-warning),
wis adds two of its own safety layers for links and one for device access.

## peek

hold **Option and click** a link to preview it in a small card without leaving
the page you are on. the preview is **incognito**, loaded in a separate ephemeral
data store and routed through your workspace proxy, so a link-based scam can
never touch your real session or browser.

- a banner warns you about suspicious links, using structural heuristics:
  homograph and punycode tricks, `user@host` URLs, deceptive anchor text, raw IP
  hosts, plain `http`, and more.
- a **reader toggle** strips the previewed page down to its content, in place.
- opening a high-risk link as a real tab first requires confirming a red "proceed
  anyway" dialog.

## navigation safety interstitial

peek handles links you choose to preview; the navigation guard handles real
navigations you might not have meant. when you click a risky link, wis intercepts
it **before anything loads in the background** and raises a full-window
interstitial showing the threat level and the reasons.

from there you can "take me back" or confirm a red "proceed anyway" (which
remembers the host for the session). a page-load fallback also catches risky
navigations that do not come from a click, like an address-bar entry or a
JavaScript redirect. because wis already enforces HTTPS-First, a plain-`http`
medium-risk page is intentionally not interrupted.

## camera and microphone permission

an embedded WebKit grants every camera and microphone request silently. wis puts
that behind your consent instead. the first time a site asks to capture, an
in-browser prompt appears anchored to the page; nothing reaches the camera or mic
until you allow it.

- the prompt carries a **"remember this decision"** toggle (on by default). a
  remembered answer persists across restarts; "just once" lasts only for the
  session.
- manage remembered grants in **settings → privacy → site permissions**: flip
  allow and block, or remove a site so it asks again.

:::note
this is macOS-only (other platforms deny), and the OS still shows its own
one-time prompt for wis itself the first time the app captures.
:::

tab folders, pinned tabs, tmux-style split panes, numbered switching, and sessions that survive a restart.

wis gives you two layouts for tabs, a collapsible **sidebar** and a horizontal
**top-tabs** strip, and the same organising tools work identically in both.

## tab folders

group open tabs into named, recolorable folders. folders organise *live* tabs,
which is different from [bookmarks](/docs/features/bookmarks/) (those save URLs
for later).

- in the **sidebar**, folders are an IDE-style tree: a colored name pill, a
  chevron, and member rows beside an accent rail.
- in the **top-tabs** strip, folders are islands: a colored circle when
  collapsed, an expanded glass pill when open.

create, rename inline, recolor, collapse, and delete folders (deleting one keeps
its tabs open, just unfiled). drag a tab onto a folder to file it, drag it out to
unfile, or use the tab's context menu. you can also give a folder an **icon**, a
wireframe or filled glyph or an emoji, rendered inside its color dot.

clicking a folder **selects** it as the target that new tabs file into, so
Cmd+T, opened links, and opened bookmarks all land in the selected folder. the
explicit "new tab" button always makes a loose, top-level tab.

collapsing a folder puts its tabs to sleep immediately, which ties into the
[memory model](#sleeping-tabs).

## pinned tabs

pin a tab to pull it out of the normal list into a docked, quick-access set
that is present in every layout. in the sidebar, pins are a favicon grid under
the workspace pill; in the top-tabs strip, they are favicon circles docked
nearest the rail. pinned tabs never sleep and never sit inside a folder. pin or
unpin from the tab context menu, or with **Cmd+Shift+P**.

## split panes

split the current view into a tmux-style tree of panes, each its own live
webview, with resizable dividers and a highlighted focused leaf.

- **Cmd+D** splits right, **Cmd+Shift+D** splits down.
- **Alt+Cmd+←/→/↑/↓** moves focus between panes.
- **Alt+Cmd+W** closes the focused pane; **Alt+Cmd+U** unsplits.

clicking a pane focuses it, and keyboard shortcuts route to the focused leaf.

## switching tabs

- **Cmd+1** through **Cmd+8** jump to a tab by its on-screen position. numbering
  follows reading order (members of expanded folders, then loose tabs) and skips
  pinned tabs and collapsed-folder members, so filing a tab renumbers the rest.
- **Cmd+9** is a ping-pong to the previously active tab.
- **Cmd+Shift+]** and **Cmd+Shift+[** cycle next and previous across every tab.
- the [command palette](/docs/features/productivity/#command-palette) (Cmd+L)
  switches to any tab by name.

## reopen, duplicate, move

- **Cmd+Shift+T** reopens the last closed tab with its **full session** intact:
  history, scroll position, and form contents are all restored. reopen is
  folder-faithful, dropping the tab back into the folder it came from. (reopen is
  inert in private workspaces.)
- **Cmd+Shift+K** duplicates the current tab.
- the tab context menu can **move a tab to a new window** or to another
  workspace, carrying its session along.

## sleeping tabs

to keep wis light, background tabs are **discarded** ("slept") after an idle
threshold and recreated when you return to them. at launch only visible tabs
spin up a webview; the rest load on first show.

waking a slept tab is not a cold reload: its full back/forward history, scroll
position, and form data are restored from a saved snapshot. those sessions also
**survive a full restart**, captured periodically to disk.

the active tab, pinned tabs, audibly-playing tabs, and any
[popped-out video](/docs/features/media/) never sleep. tabs in a collapsed
folder sleep immediately. tune the idle threshold in **settings → performance**.

a quick-launch dock of social and AI apps that open in a floating side panel without leaving your tab.

widgets are a quick-launch dock of your favourite web apps, social and AI, that
open in a floating panel beside your tabs. it is a fast way to glance at WhatsApp
or ask ChatGPT something without opening a tab or losing your place.

## the dock

choose your widgets in **settings → sidebar widgets** (toggle chips, grouped
social and AI). the dock renders in every layout: two rows in the sidebar, a
vertical column in the top-tabs rail. drag the favicons to reorder them; that
order is the display order everywhere.

the catalog covers common social and messaging apps and the major AI providers.
favicons are prefetched and cached, with a letter-tile fallback.

## the widget panel

click a widget to open it in a panel that floats above your tabs on the side
nearest the rail (Opera-style). the panel shares the current workspace's session,
so your logins persist, its proxy, and the same tracker filtering as your tabs.

- **switching widgets is instant**: panels stay loaded and hidden, so each keeps
  its own in-page state (drafts, scroll, live connections).
- a header bar shows the current host and offers **mute** and **reload**.
- drag the panel's inner edge to resize it; the width is remembered.
- the panel is **not a tab**: it dismisses when you click outside it, press
  Escape, click into a page, or switch tabs. dismissing hides it, so reopening is
  instant; a backgrounded panel also suspends its media so it never plays out of
  sight.

## memory control

each panel is a full page, which can cost anywhere from ~100 MB to a couple of
gigabytes for a heavy app like WhatsApp Web. wis keeps that in check, all in
**settings → performance**:

- a **panel limit** (default 2) caps how many stay loaded, evicting the
  least-recently-used; turn it off for no limit.
- **keep loaded** (default on) decides whether a dismissed panel keeps its
  webview; off reclaims it immediately (your login still persists).
- kept-loaded panels are reclaimed after an idle window, and a
  **memory-pressure cap** evicts the heaviest hidden panels when their combined
  footprint crosses a limit.
- a **loaded panels** readout lists what is open, with a "close all" button.

mute is engine-level and keyed per widget, so a muted messaging widget stays
silent, pings included, across reopen.

color-accented profiles with their own session, proxy, and privacy mode, plus private windows and per-workspace backgrounds.

a workspace is a self-contained browsing profile. each one has its own WebView
data store (cookies, logins, local storage), its own network proxy, and its own
privacy mode, so work and personal never touch. workspaces are color-accented,
and the accent threads through the chrome so you always know which one you are
in.

## one window per workspace

wis is **one OS window per workspace**. in-window multitasking is the
[split pane](/docs/features/tabs-and-panes/#split-panes); separate windows are
separate workspaces.

- **new window** opens a picker of workspaces no window is currently showing,
  plus a "new empty workspace" row.
- **move to new window** (on the tab context menu) tears a tab out into its own
  window, carrying its history and scroll.
- **move to workspace** relocates a tab into another existing workspace.

if you try to switch to a workspace that another window already shows, wis
focuses that window instead of duplicating it. your open windows are restored on
the next launch, each at the size and position you left it.

## private browsing

a private window is an **ephemeral workspace**: its data store is non-persistent,
it is excluded from every save, and it is wiped the moment you close it. nothing
from a private workspace ever touches disk.

- **new private window** opens one immediately, no picker.
- private windows wear a closed-eye owl icon, in the title bar and in the Dock,
  as a quiet signal that wis is not watching.
- bookmarks, session restore, and saved passwords are all disabled in private
  workspaces by design.

you can also set wis to **always launch private** if you want every session to
start clean.

## per-workspace backgrounds

each workspace can carry its own page background, set in **settings → appearance
→ workspace background**.

- **gradients**: pick an angle and two to eight color stops, each with a custom
  color picker. edits preview live.
- **wallpapers and GIFs**: import a PNG, JPEG, GIF, or WebP (up to 20 MB). tune
  the fit (cover, contain, or tile), a dim overlay, and a blur that softens the
  wallpaper without blurring your content. GIFs animate.

across split panes a wallpaper is laid out as one shared image, so the panes
reveal contiguous regions of the same picture rather than repeating it. each
mode (theme default, gradient, image) remembers its own last configuration, so
switching between them restores what you built in each.

## custom accents

the workspace color popover offers a grid of preset accents plus a saved custom
palette. the dashed `+` square opens the color picker to mint a new accent;
confirming it both saves the color to your shared palette and applies it to the
workspace.

build and run wis locally with the Makefile, pnpm, and cargo.

wis is a Cargo workspace with a React/TypeScript chrome, wired together with
Tauri. everything runs through the `Makefile`.

## prerequisites

- a **Rust** toolchain (stable), via [rustup](https://rustup.rs/).
- **Node.js** and **pnpm**. wis is pnpm-only; never use npm, npx, or yarn.
- the platform Tauri/WebView build dependencies. on macOS that is the Xcode
  command-line tools; on Linux, the WebKitGTK and related dev packages listed in
  the [Tauri prerequisites](https://tauri.app/start/prerequisites/).

## clone and run

```bash
git clone https://github.com/fuyu-myk/wis.git
cd wis
make install   # install the frontend dependencies (pnpm)
make dev       # launch the app in development mode
```

`make dev` runs `pnpm tauri dev`. the built-in [Tor client](/docs/features/network-and-tor/)
is a **default cargo feature**, so a plain `make dev` already includes it.

## a production build

```bash
make build
```

this produces a bundled, optimized app for your platform's target triple. the
Makefile detects your architecture automatically (Apple Silicon, Intel, Linux,
or Windows).

## the commands

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `make install` | install frontend dependencies with pnpm |
| `make dev` | launch the app in development mode |
| `make build` | production build for your platform |
| `make check` | `cargo check` the whole workspace |
| `make test` | run the full Rust test suite |
| `make lint` | clippy with warnings as errors |
| `make fmt` | format all Rust code |
| `make clean` | remove build artefacts |

the frontend typecheck gate is `cd crates/shell && pnpm build` (which runs `tsc`
then `vite build`).

## cargo features

the **`tor`** feature is on by default. to build without the bundled Tor client:

```bash
cargo build --no-default-features
```

## where to go next

the [architecture reference](/docs/reference/architecture/) explains how the
five crates fit together and where new logic belongs, which is the best starting
point if you plan to contribute.

how wis is built, the five-crate workspace, the IPC pattern, and where new logic belongs. for contributors.

this page is a contributor-facing overview of how wis is built. the full,
authoritative architecture document is [`WIS.md`](https://github.com/fuyu-myk/wis/blob/main/WIS.md)
at the repository root; read it before making changes.

## the shape of it

wis is a **Cargo workspace** with a React/TypeScript chrome, wired together with
Tauri. the guiding principle is a **functional core, imperative shell**: pure,
dependency-light logic lives in the core crates and is fully testable, while
Tauri commands and React components stay thin.

## the five crates

dependencies flow strictly downward; upper layers import lower ones, never the
reverse.

```text
wis-browser-app  (crates/shell/src-tauri)  Tauri shell, IPC commands, native glue
       |
  wis-network    (crates/network)          privacy decision engine, proxy, DoH, Tor
       |
  wis-storage    (crates/storage)          Storage trait + SQLite
       |                 \
   wis-core      (crates/core)   wis-secrets (crates/secrets)  vault crypto + keychain
   (pure data model, no I/O)
```

- **wis-core**: the pure data model, no I/O. defines the root browser state,
  workspaces, tabs, settings, and the typed transitions over them. every mutation
  is a pure builder that returns a new value.
- **wis-secrets**: vault cryptography and master-key storage, isolated from the
  rest. ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a key held in the macOS Keychain.
- **wis-storage**: the persistence layer. a `Storage` trait with a single SQLite
  implementation; browser state is saved across normalized tables in one atomic
  transaction.
- **wis-network**: the privacy decision engine, tracker blocking, DNS over HTTPS,
  HTTPS-First, the per-workspace proxy, and the built-in Tor client.
- **wis-browser-app**: the Tauri shell. IPC commands, app state, and the native
  macOS glue (overlays, biometrics, cookies, downloads, and the rest).

## the IPC pattern

every mutating command follows the same shape: take the state lock, snapshot for
rollback, compute the next state through a pure transition from `wis-core`,
persist it, and roll back in memory if the write fails. on success the command
emits a `browser-state-changed` event and the frontend re-fetches state through
React Query, which is the single source of truth on the JavaScript side.

## the frontend

the chrome lives in `crates/shell/src`, in React and TypeScript. because native
tab webviews composite **above** the chrome, any floating UI that must sit over a
page (the find bar, command palette, URL-bar suggestions, peek, and so on) is a
separate **overlay webview**, positioned natively. the chrome bundle is
window-agnostic: it reads its own window label at runtime and routes everything
to that window, so a secondary window behaves exactly like the main one over its
own workspace.

## contributing

the [quality bar](https://github.com/fuyu-myk/wis/blob/main/WIS.md) is
production-grade or it does not ship, judged on correctness, performance,
security, UI/UX, and architecture together. before claiming a change done, run
the frontend typecheck (`cd crates/shell && pnpm build`), `make lint`, and
`make test`. a change to a core subsystem needs a test that locks the invariant.
keep `WIS.md` accurate in the same change; it is the source of truth other
contributors and agents read first.

what the system WebKit engine cannot do, and why, stated plainly.

wis renders with the operating system's WebView (WKWebView on macOS) through
Tauri and wry, the same engine as Safari. that one choice is the source of
everything wis is good at, a tiny bundle, low RAM, Safari-class speed and
battery, and no second engine to update, and it dictates the limits below. these
are **structural tradeoffs, not bugs**, and we would rather state them plainly
than pretend they are not there.

## premium DRM video (Widevine)

WKWebView's only content decryption module is Apple's FairPlay, not Google's
Widevine, and there is no API to inject a Widevine module. FairPlay itself is not
licensed for general third-party-app playback, and services like Netflix gate on
the Safari app specifically.

the result: premium DRM streaming (Netflix, Disney+, and similar, especially at
1080p or 4K) is degraded or blocked. the mitigation is the
[open in default browser](/docs/features/productivity/#open-in-default-browser)
action, which hands the page to Safari, not an in-app fix. adding native Widevine
would mean bundling a Chromium engine plus a Widevine license, which would forfeit
the bundle, RAM, and battery wins that make wis what it is, so it is explicitly
not pursued. (even Firefox forks like Zen punt DRM to Firefox for the same
licensing reason.)

wis does enable WebKit's **Media Source and Encrypted Media Extensions** (see
[media extensions](/docs/features/network-and-tor/#media-extensions-mse-and-eme)),
which restores adaptive streaming on many non-DRM sites and exposes FairPlay to
services that request it. that does not unlock Widevine-gated services, and
Safari-app-gated FairPlay services still refuse.

## browser extensions

an embedded WKWebView cannot load Safari Web Extensions; those are reserved for
Safari. instead of a WebExtensions runtime, wis ships a native blocking stack,
content-rule blocking, an ad-blocking engine, cosmetic filtering, scriptlets, and
an element picker, plus a Tampermonkey-style user-script runner. see
[privacy and blocking](/docs/features/privacy-and-blocking/) for what that covers.

## site isolation

WebKit's site isolation is weaker than Chrome's (it is still rolling out
upstream). this is offset by strong OS sandboxing and out-of-process rendering.

## other gaps

- **no cross-device sync** and **no mobile companion**.
- some newer web APIs (WebUSB, WebBluetooth, web push, PWA install) are partial
  or absent under WebKit.
- native feature parity, system-data cookies, biometrics, page zoom, and the
  default-browser handoff, is **macOS-only** today. wis builds and runs on Linux
  and Windows, but those pieces are not yet at parity.
